{{Short description|Immediate inference concept in logic}}
'''Subalternation'''<ref>{{cite book |title=A Concise Introduction to Logic 4th edition |last=Hurley |first=Patrick |year=1991 |publisher=Wadsworth Publishing |page=192 |url=https://archive.org/details/studyguidetoacco00burc|url-access=registration }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Copi |first=Irving M. |last2=Cohen |first2=Carl |title=Introduction to Logic |publisher=Prentice Hall |year=2005 |page=189 }}</ref> is an [[immediate inference]] which is only made between '''A''' (All '''S''' are '''P''') and '''I''' (Some '''S''' are '''P''') [[categorical proposition]]s and between '''E''' (No '''S''' are '''P''' or originally, No '''S''' is '''P''') and '''O''' (Some '''S''' are not '''P''' or originally, Not every '''S''' is '''P''') categorical propositions of the traditional [[square of opposition]] and the original square of opposition.<ref>{{cite encyclopedia |first=Terence |last=Parsons |editor=Edward N. Zalta |year=2012 |title=The Traditional Square of Opposition |encyclopedia=The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy |edition=Fall 2012 |url=http://plato.stanford.edu/archives/fall2012/entries/square#IrrSyl |at=3-4}}</ref> If the '''A''' proposition is true we may immediately infer that '''I''' is true. If the '''E''' proposition is true we may immediately infer that '''O''' is true.  [[Converse (logic)|Conversely]], If the '''I''' is false, we can immediately infer that '''A''' is also false, as well as if '''O''' is false, then '''E''' is false. However, if the '''A''' proposition is false that will not tell us anything about the truth value of the '''I''' proposition. Similarly, if the '''E''' proposition is false, that will not tell us anything about the truth value of the '''O''' proposition.

An example of a subalternation is "If all leopards are mammals, then some leopards are mammals."

When the inference is misapplied, the [[syllogistic fallacy]] is called an [[illicit subalternation]].
